title: Episodic Pivot
teaches: The Episodic Pivot as we trade it: a neglected stock, flat or down for months, is re-priced by a named surprise on huge volume; the gap holds and closes in the upper half; the buy is at market over the opening-range high on day one, or over the gap-day high on a delayed entry while the gap holds; the stop sits a few cents under the day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the 9 EMA trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: Earnings EP are easiest to understand and act on.
facts.claim: Bonde: earnings EPs are the easiest to understand and act on.

facts.quote: Earnings breakout on companies with significant analyst coverage do not do as well as the first kinds.
facts.claim: Bonde: widely covered companies do not do as well.

facts.quote: Float below 25 million is ideal for this. The best moves happen on float below 10 million.
facts.claim: Bonde: a float under 25 million is ideal, the best under 10 million.

facts.quote: In many cases the volume on earnings day might be the highest volume in the history of the stock or multi year high volume.
facts.claim: Bonde: the earnings-day volume is often the highest in the stock's history.

facts.quote: typically of 10 times or more compared to average volume
facts.claim: Bonde: the big winners trade 10 times average volume or more.

facts.quote: Most EP where I made big money I bought in pre market.
facts.claim: Bonde bought his biggest EPs pre-market.

facts.quote: During the day Run EP scan c/c1>1.04 and v>3*avgv50.1 and v>=300000 multiple times , see if there is stock with neglect+ game changing earnings
facts.claim: Bonde's 2014 scan: 3 times the 50-day volume, then look for neglect plus game-changing earnings.

facts.quote: EP is a very specific pattern post earnings that shows up on stocks with years of neglect.
facts.claim: Bonde: the EP shows up on stocks with years of neglect.

facts.quote: You want to see stock with neglect, that has significant first or second earnings surprise.
facts.claim: Bonde: neglect plus a first or second earnings surprise.

facts.quote: A genuinely surprising earnings in most cases leads to big gap up and huge pre market volume.
facts.claim: Bonde: a genuine surprise leads to a big gap and huge pre-market volume.

facts.quote: Also out of those stocks I only focus on those which had Episodic Pivots for the first time in last six months.
facts.claim: Bonde focuses on the first EP in six months.

facts.quote: Similarly Episodic Pivots at begining of move are more valuable than later.
facts.claim: Bonde: an EP at the beginning of a move is worth more than a later one.

facts.quote: The stock should move immediately (within 5 days) after Episodic Pivot, otherwise you go on to next opportunity.
facts.claim: Bonde: the stock should move within 5 days, or move on.

facts.quote: I am looking for stocks which have not rallied in anticipation of earnings.
facts.claim: Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied into earnings.

facts.quote: I only track companies whose earnings are up 100% or more quarter over quarter and the earnings should be at least 5 cents.
facts.claim: Bonde tracked earnings up 100% or more.

facts.quote: When market expectations are low, or market has had several months of correction, you will find 50 to 100 opportunities in an earning season.
facts.claim: Bonde: after a correction, 50 to 100 opportunities in an earnings season.

facts.quote: Even in bear markets you will find opportunities using this strategy.
facts.claim: Bonde: the strategy finds opportunities even in bear markets.

facts.quote: Neglect will reflect in no big rally pre earnings. A extended sideways trading period or a down move coming in to earnings.
facts.claim: Bonde: neglect looks like no rally before earnings, a long sideways period or a down move.

facts.quote: Third and fourth earnings surprise most of the time are priced in or are tricky as they often lead to big gap and then reversal.
facts.claim: Bonde: a third or fourth surprise is often priced in and reverses after the gap.

facts.quote: But if the gaps are more than 20%, the stocks pull back most of the time. Smaller gaps are better.
facts.claim: Bonde: gaps over 20% pull back most of the time; smaller gaps are better.

facts.quote: The central idea behind the Episodic Pivot is a big price or volume move plus some episode.
facts.claim: Bonde: an EP is a big price or volume move plus an episode.

facts.quote: James Crammer, Barron's, WSJ, and other publication mentions, analyst upgrade etc. have a low probability of follow through.
facts.claim: Bonde: publication mentions and analyst upgrades have a low probability of follow-through.

facts.quote: Earnings, new product, analyst earnings change, increased earnings guidance, sector moves etc have high probability to trigger multi month rallies.
facts.claim: Bonde: earnings, new products and raised guidance are the high-probability catalysts.

facts.quote: The most explosive Episodic Pivots occur in stocks that have Gone Public in the last 10 years and have a capitalization of less than $ 10 billion once they enter their growth phase.
facts.claim: Bonde: the most explosive EPs are young companies under $10 billion.

facts.quote: What is an EP? My definition (this may differ from Pradeeps) is a gap up of 10% or more.
facts.claim: Kullamagi defines his EP as a gap up of 10% or more.

facts.quote: An EP needs to be a gap of 10%+ and big volume should be there, if not in pre-market then the first 5-10 minutes after the open.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a 10% gap with big volume by the first minutes after the open.

facts.quote: Now the middle red arrow, the stock gapped up slightly but sold off. This is not an EP.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a gap that sells off is not an EP.

facts.quote: There has to be massive volume near the open, ideally the stock should trade the average daily volume the first 15-20 minutes or even quicker.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the average daily volume should trade in the first 15 to 20 minutes.

facts.quote: The best EPs are on stocks ones that have gone sideways for 3-6 months or more.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the best EPs come after 3 to 6 months sideways.

facts.quote: It’s best if the stock has not rallied over the past 3-6 months.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: best if the stock has not rallied in the past 3 to 6 months.

facts.quote: these can work but the failure rate is higher and the move probably won’t be as big.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: a second EP can work, but fails more and moves less.

facts.quote: Ideally triple digit year over year (YoY) earnings and sales growth but mid/high double digits works really well too.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: ideally triple-digit growth; mid to high double digits works too.

facts.quote: Enter opening range highs. ORH can be the highs of the first 1-, 5-, or 60-minute candle. The stop is at the lows of the day.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: enter over the opening-range high; the stop is the low of the day.

facts.quote: I rarely trade in extended hours but prefer to wait for the opening range highs
facts.claim: Kullamagi rarely trades extended hours; he waits for the opening-range high.

facts.quote: Stop is always at the lows of the day.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is always the low of the day.

facts.quote: Make sure your stop is no more than 1x, or maximum 1.5x the average daily range or the average true range.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop no wider than one, at most 1.5, average daily ranges.

facts.quote: Trail your stop with the 10- or 20-day moving average once they surpass your initial stop.
facts.claim: Kullamagi trails the 10- or 20-day average.

facts.quote: I have personally found most success in earnings EP as they are easy to find and easy to understand.
facts.claim: Kullamagi had most success with earnings EPs.

facts.quote: Volume is the #1 thing to focus on.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: volume is the number one thing.

facts.quote: When unexpected good news hits a stock, especially if that stock is neglected, that can trigger multi-month, and multi-year moves.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: unexpected good news on a neglected stock can start a multi-month move.

facts.quote: It will take you 3-4 earnings seasons to get good at trading EP
facts.claim: Kullamagi: it takes 3 to 4 earnings seasons to get good at EPs.

facts.quote: None of them work all the time, the failure rate is high, but they all provide excellent risk rewards.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the failure rate is high; the risk-reward is what pays.

facts.quote: Buyable gap-ups should occur within an uptrend or constructive consolidation, not while a stock is in a downtrend.
facts.claim: Morales: a buyable gap-up comes in an uptrend or a constructive base, not a downtrend.

facts.quote: A buyable gap-up should hold above the intraday low of the gap-up day, and one can therefore use the intraday low of the gap-up day as a selling guide.
facts.claim: Morales: the gap-up day's intraday low is the selling guide.

facts.quote: Breakaway gaps are exciting. These occur when the price action is breaking out of a trading range or congestion area.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a breakaway gap breaks out of a trading range.

facts.quote: Avoid falling into the trap of thinking this type of gap, if associated with good volume, will be filled soon.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: a breakaway gap on good volume is not expected to fill soon.

facts.quote: Exhaustion gaps happen near the end of a good up or downtrend.
facts.claim: ChartSchool: an exhaustion gap comes near the end of a trend.

facts.quote: Buy an upward breakout only if the market and industry are trending higher.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: buy the earnings breakout only when the market and industry trend higher.

facts.quote: Select patterns with heavy announcement day volume, above the 30-day average.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: heavy announcement-day volume, above the 30-day average.

facts.quote: I love trading earnings gappers on day one.
facts.claim: The owner loves trading earnings gappers on day one.

facts.quote: We want to see bull gaps stay open because it shows who is in control of the strength.
facts.claim: The owner: we want bull gaps to stay open; it shows who is in control.

facts.quote: EP on earnings followed by a mini shakeout and classic 3 day delayed reaction.
facts.claim: The owner on BFLY: an EP on earnings, a mini shakeout, a classic 3-day delayed reaction.

facts.quote: Can enter there and place a stop at LOD and see how far it goes.
facts.claim: The owner on GRRR's gap: enter there, stop at the low of the day.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: The stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.
facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: B23: only stocks at $10 or more trading at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long; shorts only below it.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA.
facts.claim: We skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA: too stretched to buy.

facts.quote: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
facts.claim: C31: buy leaders, an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part into a climax run on your own long.

facts.quote: Prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings; the chart comes first.
facts.claim: D40: growing sales and earnings preferred; the chart comes first.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: Later sells are a judgment too: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.
facts.claim: Later sells are a judgment: sell more into strength on a later push, and trail what is left.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work
facts.claim: F68: after a correction, start with a few positions and add as they work.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: E56: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on one stock.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: D38: A and B at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: A5: the full size at one price with one stop; no adding.

facts.quote: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
facts.claim: D39: entry, stop and size written before the open.

facts.quote: A named surprise released after the close or before the open: earnings and guidance first, then a contract or partnership, a regulatory or FDA decision. Write it in the plan. No named catalyst, no EP.
facts.claim: The catalyst: a named surprise, earnings first; no named catalyst, no EP.

facts.quote: A gap over 25% is graded down, B- at best, not banned.
facts.claim: A gap over 25% is graded down to B- at best, not banned.

facts.quote: The gap day trades at least 3 times its 50-day average volume, and by the buy it is on pace: the full average daily volume has traded within the first 30 minutes.
facts.claim: Volume: at least 3 times the 50-day average, and the full average daily volume inside the first 30 minutes.

facts.quote: The A+ version: 5 times the average or more, or the highest volume in years (a High Volume Edge day).
facts.claim: The A+ volume: 5 times the average or the highest in years.

facts.quote: Neglect: the close before the gap is no more than 25% above its close 126 sessions earlier, and no more than 15% above its close 63 sessions earlier.
facts.claim: Neglect: at most 25% above the close 126 sessions earlier and 15% above the close 63 sessions earlier.

facts.quote: The first EP: no qualifying EP in the prior 126 sessions.
facts.claim: The first EP: no qualifying EP in the prior 126 sessions.

facts.quote: The gap day closes in the upper half of its range and never trades back to the prior close. If buying intraday, price is above the open and above the opening-range high at the buy.
facts.claim: The gap day closes in the upper half and never trades back to the prior close.

facts.quote: A close in the top quarter of the range is a grade cue, not a gate.
facts.claim: A close in the top quarter is a grade cue, not a gate.

facts.quote: Earnings EPs: EPS or sales growth of at least 25% year over year with a beat is the cue; triple-digit growth and a raised guide are A+ cues. A grading cue, not a gate.
facts.claim: Fundamentals: growth of at least 25% with a beat is the cue; triple-digit growth and a raised guide are A+ cues.

facts.quote: An A+ cue: a young, small company, listed under 10 years, under $10 billion in value, with a low float.
facts.claim: An A+ cue: a young, small, low-float company.

facts.quote: Day one: after the first 5-minute candle (or the first 30 minutes for a slower start), buy at market when price trades above the opening-range high, the volume is on pace
facts.claim: Day one: buy at market over the opening-range high with the volume on pace.

facts.quote: No buy more than 4% above the opening-range high, or above the delayed trigger.
facts.claim: No chase: no buy more than 4% above the opening-range high or the delayed trigger.

facts.quote: No pre-market or after-hours buys, though Bonde made his biggest EP money pre-market.
facts.claim: No pre-market or after-hours buys, although Bonde made his biggest money pre-market.

facts.quote: while the gap holds (no trade below the gap-day low, no fill to the prior close), buy at market the first tight trigger with a stop within 3%: a break of the gap-day high
facts.claim: The delayed entry: while the gap holds, buy at market the first tight trigger, a break of the gap-day high or of an inside day's high.

facts.quote: Not after three green days in a row. A guide, not a gate.
facts.claim: Not after three green days in a row; a guide, not a gate.

facts.quote: Day one: a few cents under the low of the day at the time of entry.
facts.claim: The day-one stop: a few cents under the low of the day at the time of entry.

facts.quote: Delayed entry: a few cents under the trigger day's low.
facts.claim: The delayed-entry stop: a few cents under the trigger day's low.

facts.quote: If the honest stop is wider than about 3%, skip the trade rather than tighten it.
facts.claim: A stop wider than about 3%: skip rather than tighten.

facts.quote: Before entry: the gap fills (a trade back to the prior close) on day one, or the gap-day low breaks. Step aside.
facts.claim: A gap fill on day one, or a break of the gap-day low before entry: step aside.

facts.quote: Day one: the stock gaps up and sells off below the open. Not an EP.
facts.claim: Day one: a gap that sells off below the open is not an EP.

facts.quote: The volume is not there by the first 30 minutes.
facts.claim: Invalidation: the volume is not there by the first 30 minutes.

facts.quote: No named catalyst, or a low-probability one: a media mention, an analyst upgrade alone.
facts.claim: Invalidation: no named catalyst, or a weak one such as a mention or an upgrade alone.

facts.quote: A second EP after a big run, or a stock up 50% or more in the prior 6 months: graded down hard.
facts.claim: A second EP after a big run, or up 50% or more in 6 months: graded down hard.

facts.quote: Green and Yellow: allowed (Yellow smaller and fewer). Orange: only A+ EPs. Red: mostly cash and shorts. A guide, not a hard cap.
facts.claim: Market reading: Green and Yellow allowed; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: Earnings season: most EPs come in a window of 3 to 4 weeks each quarter.
facts.claim: Most EPs come in a 3 to 4 week window each quarter.

facts.quote: EPs often work when the indexes do not. Teach them as the first longs to try as a correction ends, inside the house filter.
facts.claim: EPs are the first longs to try as a correction ends.

facts.quote: An EP comes from a neglected stock, flat or down over six months, often under its averages, and gaps 10% or more; a PEG is an established leader gapping 4% or more out of a base it was already building.
facts.claim: The PEG tell: an EP is a neglected stock; a PEG is an established leader gapping out of a base.

facts.quote: An HVE is a record-volume up day, gap or no gap, whose close is a level to mark for a day-2 reclaim; an EP is a 10% gap on 3x average volume bought the same day over the opening-range high.
facts.claim: The HVE tell: an HVE is a record-volume day, gap or no gap; an EP needs the gap.

facts.quote: A Kicker needs a weak red close and then a gap of only 1.5% or more, rarely on earnings; an EP has a named catalyst and a 10% gap, and the prior day can be any color.
facts.claim: The Kicker tell: a Kicker needs a weak red close and a small gap; an EP needs a named catalyst.

facts.quote: An EP holds its gap and closes in the upper half; a News Failure gaps up on good news and closes red, under the prior close. The same headline, the opposite trade.
facts.claim: The News Failure tell: an EP holds its gap; a News Failure closes red under the prior close.

facts.quote: ep.volume: only 2x to 3x the average
facts.claim: The B- row: volume only 2 to 3 times the average.

facts.quote: Taking a day-one close entry with the gap-day low as the stop, 7% or more away, so the size is tiny or the 3% rule is broken. Buy early near the opening-range high or wait for the first tight pullback.
facts.claim: A named mistake: a day-one close entry with the gap-day low as the stop, far away.

facts.quote: Treating every gap as one that must fill, or fading strong gaps. Bonde: people who believe all gaps get filled have a very difficult time trading this.
facts.claim: A named mistake: treating every gap as one that must fill.

facts.quote: Selling everything in the first day or two and missing the multi-week trend.
facts.claim: A named mistake: selling everything in the first day or two.

facts.quote: ep.first_ep: the first EP in 6 months or more, after 3 to 6 months of sideways action or years of neglect
facts.claim: The A+ row: the first EP in 6 months or more after months of sideways action.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; sell what is left on a close below it.
facts.claim: Our default trail: the 9 EMA for fast movers, the 20 EMA for steadier ones; a close below it sells what is left.

walkthroughs.title: MOD, May 2023: neglect plus a catalyst
steps: MOD sat flat for six months, down 8%. Then a surprise earnings report gaps it 18.8% on 3.2 times volume.
It closes near the high and never fills the gap. A neglected stock plus real news: that's an EP.
Day two it opens over the gap-day high, 24.50. Buy at market, 25.00. Stop just under the day's low, 24.75.
A fill or a stop-out and the idea's dead. Instead, 3R the next session, too soon to sell. It ran to 89.9R.

walkthroughs.title: CACI, August 2004: the day-one buy
steps: CACI drifted six months, down 5%. Then August 19, 2004, an earnings gap of 11.3% on 6.7 times volume.
The gap day's low sits within 3% of the price. The stop fits, so this one you can buy on day one.
Buy at market, 46.55. Stop a few cents under the low of the day, 45.42, 2.4% away.
Slower start, 3R on day 6, then a steady trend. Sell into a push and trail the rest on the 20 EMA.

walkthroughs.title: ENPH, October 2021: sell into the push, trail the rest
steps: ENPH gaps 18.5% on earnings in October 2021, on 8.3 times volume. The close is 56% up its range, upper half, just.
Day three it breaks the post-gap high, 227.59. Buy at market, 227.60. Stop 224.95, 1.2% under.
3R the next session, too soon to sell. Stop to breakeven. Sell into a push, trail the rest on the 9 EMA.
Later it tops and collapses back through the old stop. The sells and the trail kept it a win.

questions.q: Someone at the desk says "that one's an EP." What are they describing?
choices: A dead stock re-priced by big news
A leader gapping up out of its base
A stock on its third gap up in a year
A slow drift up along the 50-day
questions.answer: A dead stock re-priced by big news
questions.why: A dead stock re-priced by big news. That's the whole setup in one line. The stock's been flat or down for months and nobody cares about it. Then a real surprise hits. Because it never rallied into the news, none of that news is in the price yet. So the gap is the market re-pricing it in one morning, and that's why the move can run for weeks. Before I call anything an EP, I look at the six months before the gap.
questions.lesson_line: Neglect plus a real surprise. That's the whole idea.

wrong.A leader gapping up out of its base: That's a Power Earnings Gap. The stock was already working and people were already watching it. An EP is the stock nobody was watching.
wrong.A stock on its third gap up in a year: By the third gap the story's known and mostly in the price. The EP is the first surprise, at the start of the move.
wrong.A slow drift up along the 50-day: That's a quiet trend, not a pivot. An EP is one big day where the news re-prices the stock.

questions.simple: A forgotten stock that gaps on big news. The news isn't in the price yet, so the move can run.

reasons: stable definition; two Tier 2 originators agree

deeper.counter: Bonde built the setup around stocks with years of neglect and a first or second earnings surprise. Kullamagi: unexpected good news on a neglected stock can trigger multi-month moves. Both start from the same place: the stock nobody was watching.

questions.q: A big gap on heavy volume with no news behind it isn't an Episodic Pivot.
questions.why: True. The gap and the volume are only half of it. The other half is the episode, the reason the stock got re-priced. Earnings, a raised guide, a big new product: those give buyers a reason to hold the gap for weeks. With no news you have no idea why it moved, and nothing keeps the buyers there. If I can't name the news in one line, it's not an EP.
questions.lesson_line: Name the news before you name the setup.
questions.simple: True. Without real news behind the jump, buyers have no reason to keep holding it, so it isn't an EP.

reasons: rests on the card's catalyst line, a held decision (D-032)

questions.q: How was this stock acting in the months before the news?
choices: Flat or down for months, no rally
A steady uptrend above the 20 EMA
Flat for two weeks, then a sharp rally
A new high every week into the report
questions.answer: Flat or down for months, no rally
questions.why: Flat or down for months. That's neglect, and you can see it right on this chart. MOD went sideways to down for six months, down 8% going in, then gapped 18.8% on the report. Nobody bid it up ahead of the news, so none of it was in the price. That's why the gap had room to run. A stock that rallies into the report has already priced some of it in, and you're buying what's left.
questions.lesson_line: Look left first. Months of nothing is what you want before the gap.

wrong.A new high every week into the report: That's a stock everyone's already buying. The report lands on a price that already expects good news.
wrong.Flat for two weeks, then a sharp rally: Two quiet weeks isn't neglect. The rally into the report means part of the news is already priced in.
wrong.A steady uptrend above the 20 EMA: That's a leader in a trend. Good stock, but people are watching it, and that's a different setup.

questions.simple: Flat or down for months with no rally. The news isn't in the price yet, so the gap has room to run.

reasons: stable idea; two Tier 2 originators agree

questions.story: The last bar is the gap day, on an earnings report. Everything to its left is the months before it.

deeper.counter: Bonde: neglect shows as no big rally before earnings, a long sideways stretch or a down move. Kullamagi: the best EPs come after 3 to 6 months or more of sideways trading.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: When you buy the opening-range break, the stop goes a few cents under the low of the ___ at the time of entry.
questions.why: Day. The stop goes a few cents under the low of the day at the time of entry, not exactly on it. Kullamagi: the stop is always at the lows of the day. On a delayed entry it goes under the trigger day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the low of the day.
questions.simple: On day one the stop goes a few cents under the day's low at the moment you buy, not exactly on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62, stop under the day's low)

questions.q: A forgotten stock gaps up big on earnings and holds over its open on heavy volume. Where's your day-one buy?
choices: Over the opening-range high
A limit order a bit under the open
At the close, once the gap held all day
A dip back to yesterday's close
questions.why: Over the opening-range high, with a market order. The opening range is the first 30 minutes of the day. When price trades through its high, buyers just proved they're still in charge, and you get in right there. Your stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, the LOD, which is still close. That keeps the risk small and lets the full size fit. Wait for the close and that low can be 7% or more away. A strong move that triggers clean can go earlier than 30 minutes.
questions.lesson_line: The opening range is the trigger. The low of the day is the stop.

wrong.A limit order a bit under the open: We buy with market orders. A limit under the open can sit there unfilled while the stock runs without you.
wrong.At the close, once the gap held all day: We never buy the close. By then the low of the day can be 7% or more away, and that stop's too wide.
wrong.A dip back to yesterday's close: A trade back to yesterday's close fills the gap. That's the setup failing, not a place to buy.

questions.simple: Buy at market as price trades over the opening-range high. Your stop under the low of the day stays close.

reasons: rests on the day-one trigger, a held decision (D-005)
rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, market orders)

deeper.counter: Kullamagi enters opening-range highs, using the first 1, 5 or 60-minute candle, with the stop at the lows of the day. Our default range is the first 30 minutes.

questions.q: On a big enough earnings surprise, we'll buy the EP pre-market.
questions.why: False. We don't buy before the bell. Bonde made his biggest EP money pre-market, so I get the temptation. But our buy needs a trigger and a stop, and both come from the day's own trading. The opening-range high and the low of the day don't exist until the market opens. Pre-market you'd be buying thin trading with no real stop. So wait for the open, let the range form, and buy through its high.
questions.lesson_line: No trigger before the bell, so no buy before the bell.
questions.simple: False. We only buy in regular hours, because our trigger and our stop both come from the day's own range.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E58, regular hours)

questions.q: You're going through this morning's gappers, hunting for EPs. Which kind of news do you check first?
choices: An earnings report
An FDA decision
A sector move
An analyst upgrade
questions.why: Earnings. A report is dated, public and you can measure it. You know when it's coming, and you can check the growth and the beat before you put a dollar in. That's why we start there. An earnings gap alone still isn't an EP, though. The stock needs months of neglect behind it too. Other big news can work, but the report is the first place I look.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings first. You know the date and you can read the numbers.

wrong.An FDA decision: Biotech news is the hardest kind to trade, and tough to judge from the outside. Not where you start.
wrong.A sector move: It can work, but it's news about the group, not this company. The report is easier to read, so start there.
wrong.An analyst upgrade: An upgrade on its own is weak news. It rarely gets real follow-through.

questions.simple: Start with earnings. The report is dated and public, and you can check the numbers before you buy.

reasons: two Tier 2 originators agree on a stable point

deeper.counter: Bonde: earnings EPs are the easiest to understand and act on, and he lists sector moves among the high-probability catalysts too. Kullamagi had most success with earnings EPs and calls biotech EPs the most difficult.

questions.q: It's 10:30 and you haven't bought yet. What's the play?
choices: Pass, it's not an EP anymore
Buy the first bounce off the low
Buy the close if it's green
Short it, the gap will fill
questions.story: A stock gaps up 11% on its report. By 10:30 it's back under its open, on heavy volume.
questions.answer: Pass, it's not an EP anymore
questions.why: Pass. A gap that falls back under its open isn't an EP. The open was the buyers' best shot. Now sellers are using the good news to get out, and heavy volume here means heavy selling too. There's no trigger to buy either, with price under the open and nowhere near the opening-range high. We want a gap that holds and closes strong. This one's telling you it won't.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that can't hold its open has told you everything. Walk away.

wrong.Buy the first bounce off the low: A bounce under the open isn't a trigger. We buy through the opening-range high, and it's nowhere near it.
wrong.Buy the close if it's green: We don't buy closes. Green or not, it already failed under its open.
wrong.Short it, the gap will fill: Betting every gap fills is a named mistake. Not an EP means no long. It doesn't hand you a short.

questions.simple: Pass. When a gap falls under its open, the sellers are winning and there's no trigger left to buy.

reasons: card line plus Kullamagi's own example

questions.q: A gap day that closes in the lower half of its range still counts as an EP if the volume was huge.
questions.why: False. The gap day must close in the upper half of its range and never trade back to the prior close. Volume grades the day, but the close is a gate. We want bull gaps to stay open. It shows who is in control of the strength.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close cancels huge volume. The close is a gate.
questions.simple: False, because the close must be in the upper half of the range, however big the volume was.

reasons: card gate; the same gate as q12 and q65

questions.q: What volume test does a day-one buy have to pass?
choices: The average daily volume by 10:00
Double the average by the close
Half the average daily volume by 10:00
The average daily volume by lunch
questions.why: The average daily volume by 10:00 Eastern, which is the first 30 minutes. Our card wants the gap day at 3 times the 50-day average volume. By the buy, the full average daily volume must also be on pace to trade within the first 30 minutes. Kullamagi: ideally within 15 to 20 minutes or even quicker. Volume is the number one thing.
questions.lesson_line: On pace means a whole day's volume before the coffee is cold.

wrong.Double the average by the close: Double by the close is a B- day on our card, and it is known too late for a day-one buy.
wrong.The average daily volume by lunch: By lunch is too slow. The test is the first 30 minutes, or quicker.
wrong.Half the average daily volume by 10:00: Half a day is not on pace. Our card wants the full average daily volume within the first 30 minutes.

questions.simple: The full average day of volume must trade in the first 30 minutes, which means by 10:00 Eastern.

deeper.trap: The test is a pace, not a final tally. Kullamagi wants the average daily volume to trade in the first 15 to 20 minutes or even quicker. Our card allows the first 30 minutes, so a stock that reaches it only by 10:00 is on the slow edge of the test.

reasons: card test; Kullamagi's quote agrees

questions.q: How does this second gap stack up against the first one?
choices: Weaker, second EPs fail more often
Stronger, the first proved the story
The same, every gap starts fresh
No setup, a contract isn't news
questions.story: Three months ago a stock had a textbook EP: a 14% earnings gap on 4x volume that held. It has run since. Now it gaps 12% on 4x volume on a new contract win.
questions.answer: Weaker, second EPs fail more often
questions.why: Weaker. The first gap did the re-pricing. Three months and a big run later, the stock isn't forgotten anymore. Part of any good news is already in the price. A second EP can still work. It just fails more often, and the move tends to be smaller. So I'd grade it down and be pickier on the entry. The first surprise on a stock nobody owns is the one that pays best.
questions.lesson_line: A second surprise is worth less. The first one already moved the price.

wrong.Stronger, the first proved the story: The first gap already moved the stock. The more it's run, the more of the news is in the price.
wrong.The same, every gap starts fresh: It doesn't start fresh. Everyone knows the name now, and that's the edge gone.
wrong.No setup, a contract isn't news: A contract is real, named news. The problem is the run before it, not the catalyst.

questions.simple: Weaker. The stock's been re-priced once already, so more of the good news is in the price.

deeper.counter: Bonde looks for neglect plus a first or second earnings surprise, so a second gap alone does not end his trade. Kullamagi says an EP after an earlier one can work, but fails more and moves less.

reasons: rests on the card's first-EP line (c06), a held pick
re-asked as the card's test, not as a ban

questions.q: Who won the gap day, and how can you tell?
choices: Buyers, it closed near the high
Sellers, they faded it off the high
Nobody, it closed mid-range
Too early to tell from one day
questions.answer: Buyers, it closed near the high
questions.why: Buyers. SIG closed at 91% of its range, right near the high, and the gap stayed wide open. That tells you who held the stock into the bell. Plenty of people had a profit to take that day, and the buyers soaked it all up. That's what you want from a gap day. A close near the low says sellers took it back and the market isn't buying the news.
questions.lesson_line: Strong close, gap open. That's the buyers telling you they're staying.

wrong.Sellers, they faded it off the high: It closed at 91% of its range. A fade closes near the low, and this didn't.
wrong.Nobody, it closed mid-range: A mid-range close would be a tie. This one finished near the top of the day.
wrong.Too early to tell from one day: The gap day is the read. Where it closes is the first thing we judge.

questions.simple: Buyers. It closed near the high with the gap still open, so they held it all day.

reasons: reworded and fixed before

questions.story: The last bar is the gap day: a 12.1% gap on a deal announcement, on 10.3x volume. Check where it closed and whether the gap stayed open.

questions.q: The report is out at 7:30 and the stock is up 15% pre-market on big volume. We wait for regular hours.
questions.why: True. No new buys outside regular trading hours. The opening range forms after the bell, and so does the stop under it.
questions.lesson_line: Pre-market shows you the gap. Regular hours give you the trade.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We usually wait until day ___ at the earliest for a first sell.
questions.why: 3. We very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: First sell: day 3 at the earliest, and it is a judgment call.
questions.simple: We wait until day 3 at the earliest for a first sell, and it is a judgment call.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, first trim)

questions.q: You buy that break on day three. Where's your stop?
choices: Just under the day-three low
Under the gap-day low, it held
Under the close before the gap
Under the 9 EMA, the trail
questions.why: Just under the day-three low, a few cents under it. That's the day you bought, the trigger day. If price trades back under that low, the break failed, plain and simple. A stop right there keeps a failed break cheap and lets you size the trade properly. The gap-day low sits further down, so it only adds risk without telling you anything new. Put it in as a real stop order with your broker.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger day's low is the stop. Not the gap-day low.

wrong.Under the 9 EMA, the trail: The 9 EMA trails what's left later, on a close below it. It isn't your first stop.
wrong.Under the gap-day low, it held: That works as a line, but it's wider than you need. Our stop goes under the trigger day's low, which is tighter.
wrong.Under the close before the gap: That's a gap fill. It ends the setup before you're in, and it's way too wide for a stop.

questions.simple: Just under the day-three low, the day you bought. If it breaks that, the trade failed and the loss stays small.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62, stop first)

questions.story: Day two after an earnings gap. Tomorrow it trades over the post-gap high, and you buy that day-three break.

deeper.counter: Morales uses the gap-up day's intraday low as his selling guide. Ours sits at or above it, so ours is tighter.

questions.q: Prior close 40.00, today's open 44.80. How big is the gap, in percent?
questions.why: 12.0%. The gap is the open minus the prior close, over the prior close: (44.80 - 40.00) / 40.00 = 12%. Kullamagi defines his EP as a gap up of 10% or more, with big volume by the first minutes after the open. The gap alone does not make an EP: it also needs a named catalyst.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap from the prior close to the open. Then check the volume.
questions.simple: Take the open minus the prior close, divide by the prior close, and you get 12.0%.

reasons: computed key
the gap floor is a held decision (D-033)

wrong.10.7%: Divided the gap by the open, not by the prior close.
wrong.4.8%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.1.2%: A decimal slip. The gap is far more than a percent.

questions.q: Do you treat this one as an EP?
choices: No, a TV mention is weak news
Yes, the gap and volume are enough
Yes, any news counts
No, 15% is too small a gap
questions.story: A stock gaps up 15% on big volume. The only news is a morning television mention by a well-known host.
questions.answer: No, a TV mention is weak news
questions.why: No. A TV mention isn't an episode. Nothing changed at the company. Somebody just talked about it on air, and that kind of pop tends to fade once the crowd moves on. Earnings, a raised guide, a big new product: that's news that changes what the business is worth. The 15% gap and the volume only show you something happened. They don't give buyers a reason to stay.
questions.lesson_line: A TV mention isn't an episode. Earnings, a contract, an approval: those are.

wrong.Yes, the gap and volume are enough: Price and volume are half of it. The other half is real news, and a mention isn't.
wrong.Yes, any news counts: Not all news is equal. Mentions and upgrades on their own rarely get follow-through.
wrong.No, 15% is too small a gap: 15% is a big gap for an EP. The news is what fails here.

questions.simple: No. A TV mention changes nothing about the company, so buyers have no reason to keep holding the gap.

reasons: rests on the card's catalyst line, a held decision (D-032)

deeper.counter: Bonde: publication mentions and analyst upgrades have a low probability of follow-through. Earnings, new products and raised guidance have a high probability of triggering multi-month rallies.

questions.q: Do you take it here or wait?
choices: Buy now, stop under the low
Wait for the close to confirm
Wait for a pullback to fill the gap
Buy half now, half at the close
questions.story: A neglected stock gaps 14% on earnings, with volume on pace for 6x the average. At 9:40 it trades over the 5-minute high. The low of the day is 2.1% below.
questions.answer: Buy now, stop under the low
questions.why: Buy it. It's moving through the 5-minute high with the volume on pace, and the low of the day is only 2.1% away. That's right inside the 1 to 3% we like. Your stop goes a few cents under that low, and the full size fits at one price. Wait for the close and that stop could be miles away, so your size shrinks to nothing. Heavy volume's a plus here, not a must. The tight stop is what makes it a buy.
questions.lesson_line: A tight low under a gap that holds is the day-one buy. Take it.

wrong.Buy half now, half at the close: No starter piece. We buy the full size at one price with one stop.
wrong.Wait for the close to confirm: By the close the stop's far away and the size gets tiny. The tight entry is right now.
wrong.Wait for a pullback to fill the gap: A gap fill kills the setup. You want the gap to stay open, not close.

questions.simple: Buy now. The stop under the low of the day is only 2.1% away, and waiting would push it far off.

reasons: the day-one buy is a held decision (D-005)

questions.q: Your stop would have to go under the low. What do you do?
choices: Wait for a later, tighter trigger
Buy your usual shares with an 8% stop
Buy it and put a 3% stop under
Wait for the close, then buy it
questions.story: A stock gaps 14% on earnings on 6x volume and holds. At 10:00 it trades over the opening-range high, but the low of the day is 8% below the price.
questions.answer: Wait for a later, tighter trigger
questions.why: Wait for a later, tighter trigger. The honest stop is a few cents under the low of the day, and that's 8% away. We like 1 to 3% and we'll go up to 5%. Past 5% we mostly wait. Your size comes from the stop, so an 8% stop means a tiny position or way too much risk. And you never pull the stop up just to make it fit. As long as the gap holds, it can give you a delayed entry with a stop inside 5%.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last. A wide low means wait.

wrong.Buy your usual shares with an 8% stop: Usual shares on an 8% stop risks far more than you planned. The size has to come from the stop.
wrong.Buy it and put a 3% stop under: A 3% stop sits above the low of the day. You moved the stop to fit the trade, and normal noise takes you out.
wrong.Wait for the close, then buy it: We don't buy closes. The low of the day is still way down there, so the stop's still too wide.

questions.simple: Wait for a later trigger. An 8% stop means a tiny size or too much risk, and you never move a stop to fit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and A13)
held decision D-005 (day-one stop width)

questions.q: You were waiting to buy this one. What now?
choices: Step aside, the gap filled
Buy it, the fill is support
Buy the close if it bounces
Short it, the gap is dead
questions.story: A stock gaps 12% on earnings. By 11:00 it has traded all the way back to yesterday's close.
questions.why: Step aside. Trading back to yesterday's close fills the gap, and on day one that ends the setup. We want bull gaps to stay open because it shows who's in control. A full fill by 11:00 says the sellers took back every bit of the news in a couple of hours. A late bounce doesn't fix that. Move on to the next name.
questions.lesson_line: A gap that fills on day one had no buyers behind it.

wrong.Buy it, the fill is support: A filled gap isn't support. It's the setup failing.
wrong.Buy the close if it bounces: The fill already ended it. A bounce into the close doesn't bring it back, and we don't buy closes anyway.
wrong.Short it, the gap is dead: Dead for a long, sure. That doesn't make it a short. Nothing here sets up a short trade.

questions.simple: Step aside. Once it trades back to yesterday's close, the sellers won the day and the setup is over.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: The app's market filter reads Orange, one step above Red. Three EPs trigger today: an A+, an A and a B. Which do you buy?
choices: Just the A+
The A+ and the A
None, Orange means cash
All three, EPs ignore the market
questions.why: Just the A+. Orange means the market's under pressure, and breakouts fail more often when the market isn't behind them. So I only want my very best idea, the cleanest EP with the tightest risk. The A and the B can wait for a better market. The grade is our read on how clean the setup is, and it sets your size. Green is when we press. Red is mostly cash.
questions.lesson_line: Orange: only the cleanest setup gets your money.

wrong.The A+ and the A: In Orange the A stays out. Only the cleanest setup earns a spot.
wrong.None, Orange means cash: That's Red. Orange still lets your very best setups through.
wrong.All three, EPs ignore the market: EPs can work in rough markets, but we still follow the filter. A weak market punishes the lesser setups first.

questions.simple: Just the A+. In a weak market only your best setup is worth the risk.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)

deeper.counter: Bonde finds EP opportunities even in bear markets. Bulkowski buys the earnings breakout only when the market and industry trend higher. We keep the market filter, as a guide rather than a hard cap.

questions.q: Most EPs show up in a few weeks each quarter, during earnings season.
questions.why: True. Most EPs come in a 3 to 4 week window every quarter. That's when the reports come out, so that's when the surprises land. Build your list of neglected names before the season starts. Then hunt hard while the reports are coming out, and be patient in the quiet weeks between.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings season is EP season. Have the list ready before it starts.
questions.simple: True. Most EPs come from earnings news, and the reports come out in a few weeks each quarter.

reasons: a count that varies by season (50 to 100)

questions.q: The 50-day average volume is 2 million shares. The gap day traded 5.5 million. What is the multiple?
questions.why: 2.75 times. Divide the gap day's volume by the 50-day average: 5.5 million / 2 million = 2.75. That is under the 3 times our card wants, in the B- row for 2 to 3 times. Bonde's scan asks for 3 times the 50-day average.
questions.lesson_line: Divide the day's volume by the average. Three times is the floor.
questions.simple: 5.5 million divided by 2 million is 2.75 times, which is under the 3 times our card wants.

reasons: computed key

wrong.3.50x: Took the difference of the two volumes, not the ratio.
wrong.0.36x: Flipped it: the average divided by the gap day's volume.
wrong.7.50x: Added the two volumes instead of dividing.

questions.q: EP or Power Earnings Gap?
choices: A PEG; a leader, not neglected
An EP; the gap and volume qualify
An EP; earnings make it one
A Kicker; it gapped from a base
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. Into the report the stock had climbed 25.5% in six months and sat near its highs. It gaps 16.6% on 11.2x volume and closes at 80% of its range.
questions.answer: A PEG; a leader, not neglected
questions.why: A Power Earnings Gap. An EP needs a neglected stock, and this one had been climbing, up 25.5% over six months and near its highs. It is an established leader gapping on a report, not a forgotten stock being re-priced. Bonde wants stocks that have not rallied in anticipation of earnings. Kullamagi: it is best if the stock has not rallied in the past 3 to 6 months. The gap and the volume are strong, but they are only half the test.
questions.lesson_line: Same report, two setups. The six months before the gap decide which.

wrong.An EP; the gap and volume qualify: The gap day is strong, but the stock before it is not neglected. It had already climbed 25.5% in six months.
wrong.An EP; earnings make it one: An earnings gap on a leader at highs is the PEG. The EP is the neglected name's gap.
wrong.A Kicker; it gapped from a base: A Kicker needs a weak red close and a small gap. This one gapped 16.6% on 11.2x volume to a strong close.

questions.simple: It is a Power Earnings Gap, because a stock that already climbed into the report is a leader, not a forgotten name.

reasons: held decision D-002 (earnings gap on a neglected or an established name)
neglect line is a proposed card line

questions.q: Neglect check. The close 126 sessions ago was 20.00 and the close before the gap is 24.00. How far is it up, in percent?
questions.why: 20%. The close before the gap is 24.00 and the close 126 sessions earlier is 20.00. So (24.00 - 20.00) / 20.00 = 20%. Our card's neglect line is at most 25% over 126 sessions, so this passes that half of the test. The card also asks for at most 15% over 63 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Neglect is measured, not felt. Six months back, count how far it has come.
questions.simple: Take 24.00 over 20.00 and subtract one to get the percent up. That is 20%, under the 25% neglect line.

deeper.example: CRM, August 2020, was up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63. Both are past the card's lines of 25% and 15%, so it was not neglected. It was an established leader at highs, not an EP.

reasons: computed key
rests on a proposed card line (ep.neglect)

wrong.120.0%: Gave the ratio and forgot to subtract one.
wrong.16.7%: Divided the rise by the later close, not the earlier one.
wrong.4.0%: Used the dollar rise as if it were the percent.

questions.q: You missed day one. What do you do this morning?
choices: Buy, stop under today's low
Pass, day one was the only entry
Buy, stop under the gap-day low
Wait for a dip to the prior close
questions.story: An earnings gap of 20.3% on 27.6x volume closed at 82% of its range two days ago. Yesterday it held above the gap-day low. This morning it trades over the post-gap high, and the stop under today's low would sit 1.7% below.
questions.why: Buy it, and put the stop a few cents under today's low. Missing day one doesn't mean missing the trade. The gap held: nothing traded below the gap-day low, so buyers still own it. Now it's breaking the post-gap high, and the stop is only 1.7% away. That's inside the 1 to 3% we like, so a failed break costs you a little. DLB broke right here and ran to 17.1R at its best.
questions.lesson_line: Miss day one and you still get a shot. While the gap holds, the post-gap high is your second way in.

wrong.Pass, day one was the only entry: The delayed entry is our second way in. While the gap holds, the first break of the post-gap high is a buy.
wrong.Buy, stop under the gap-day low: That stop's wider than it needs to be. Today is the trigger day, and its low is closer.
wrong.Wait for a dip to the prior close: A trade back to the prior close fills the gap and ends the setup. That's no dip to buy.

questions.simple: Buy the break with the stop under today's low. The gap held and the stop is close, so a failed break costs little.

deeper.example: ENPH, October 2021: an 18.5% earnings gap closed at 56% of its range. On day three it broke the post-gap high, 227.59. The buy was 227.60 with the stop at 224.95, 1.2% under.

reasons: the delayed-entry window is a held decision (D-084)
rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, F62)

questions.q: Where's your stop now?
choices: 29.00, the first 30-minute low
Sell at the open, 29.20
No stop until it reclaims 29.40
Out now, the gap is past 2R
questions.story: You bought an EP at 30.00 with the stop at 29.40. Follow-up news gaps it open at 29.20, under your stop. The first 30-minute bar's low is 29.00.
questions.why: 29.00, the low of the first 30-minute bar. When a stock gaps through your stop, you don't dump it at the open. The first 30 minutes decide, and their low becomes your new stop. There's a ceiling, though: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you're out. Your risk was 30.00 down to 29.40. A stop at 29.00 loses less than twice that, so it's inside the line and it stands.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through your stop gets 30 minutes to decide. Not the open.

wrong.Sell at the open, 29.20: The gap rule gives it 30 minutes. Dumping the open means selling into the panic.
wrong.No stop until it reclaims 29.40: Never sit without a stop. The new stop is the 30-minute low, in with your broker.
wrong.Out now, the gap is past 2R: It isn't. The loss out to 29.00 is still under twice your planned risk.

questions.simple: 29.00, the 30-minute low. That loss is still less than twice the risk you planned, so you stay in.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
computed key (the 2R ceiling check)

questions.q: You're back at your desk. Can you still take it?
choices: Pass, that's a chase
Buy, the breakout is confirmed now
Buy, and just move the stop up too
Buy half size to be safe
questions.story: A gap day. The opening-range high was 50.00. You were away from the desk, and at 10:05 the stock trades 52.60.
questions.why: Pass, that's a chase. The trigger was the opening-range high at 50.00, and we never buy more than 4% over it. 52.60 is past that line. Chasing doesn't change your risk, it changes your size. The stop stays under the low of the day, so the distance grows and your shares shrink. I'd rather miss it than chase it. Next time, set an alert at the trigger before you walk away.
questions.lesson_line: I'd rather miss it than chase it.

wrong.Buy half size to be safe: Half a chase is still a chase.
wrong.Buy, the breakout is confirmed now: It's confirmed and it's too far. Both are true. Past 4% over the trigger is a chase.
wrong.Buy, and just move the stop up too: The stop is the low of the day. It doesn't move up to fit your late fill.

questions.simple: Pass. 52.60 is more than 4% over the 50.00 trigger, and chasing just shrinks your size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
computed key (52.60 against the 4% line)

questions.q: Three green days in a row before the delayed trigger is a reason to wait. A guide, not a gate.
questions.why: True. Our card says not after three green days in a row. It is a guide, not a gate, so it is a reason to wait and not a ban.
questions.lesson_line: After three green days in a row, wait. It is a guide, not a gate.
questions.simple: True. After three green days in a row our card says wait, though it is a guide and not a firm ban.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on a proposed card line (ep.not_three_green)

questions.q: If the average daily volume has not traded by the first 30 minutes, the day-one buy is off.
questions.why: True. The volume is not there by the first 30 minutes: an invalidation on day one. Kullamagi: ideally the average daily volume trades in the first 15-20 minutes or quicker.
questions.lesson_line: No crowd in the first 30 minutes, no day-one buy. The gap is only a gap.

questions.q: Is this one you can trade?
choices: No, it's under $10 and too thin
No, a contract isn't real news
Yes, the gap-day volume is huge
Yes, a small float runs harder
questions.story: A $7 stock that trades about $4 million a day gaps 20% on a contract. Even on the gap day it trades $9 million.
questions.answer: No, it's under $10 and too thin
questions.why: No. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that do at least $20 million a day. This one's $7 and trades about $4 million, and even the gap day only did $9 million. The real problem is getting out. In a thin stock your stop fills wherever it fills, and your own order can move the price on you. A perfect setup you can't get out of isn't a trade.
questions.lesson_line: A perfect EP in a thin stock is still a thin stock.

wrong.No, a contract isn't real news: A contract is real, named news. The stock fails on price and liquidity, not the catalyst.
wrong.Yes, the gap-day volume is huge: Huge for this stock is $9 million. That's still under our $20 million line.
wrong.Yes, a small float runs harder: A small float isn't the same as liquidity. It still has to trade $20 million a day.

questions.simple: No. It's under $10 and too thin to get in and out of at your price.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, liquidity), a held decision (D-030)

deeper.counter: Bonde liked a float under 25 million, with the best moves under 10 million. Float counts the shares out there, not the dollars traded, so it never replaces our liquidity line.

questions.q: Bought at 514.01 with the stop at 507.19. Where is 3R?
questions.why: $534.47. One R is the fill minus the stop: 514.01 minus 507.19. Add three of those to the fill, 514.01, and you get 534.47. 3R is a measuring mark, not a fixed sell. UI reached 3R the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R price before the open. It is a measuring mark, not a sell order.
questions.simple: One R is the gap between your fill and your stop. Add three of those to the fill to find 3R.

reasons: computed key

wrong.$527.65: Added the three R to the stop instead of the fill.
wrong.$493.55: Subtracted the three R instead of adding them.

questions.story: Bought on the day-two break after an earnings gap.

questions.q: Once your EP is up somewhere between 2R and 5R, you can move the stop to breakeven.
questions.why: True. Somewhere from 2R to 5R, or at your first sell, the stop can come up to breakeven. Exactly where is your call. Once it's there, a pullback can't turn a good trade into a loser. That frees you to sit through the normal shakes and let the move work. The stop only ever moves up, never down.
questions.lesson_line: Get the stop to breakeven somewhere from 2R to 5R. Then let it work.
questions.simple: True. Between 2R and 5R the stop can go to breakeven, so a pullback can't turn the winner into a loss.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)
reworded: the old 'by default at the first trim' had no source

questions.q: What do you do with the shares you have left?
choices: Sell, it closed under the 9 EMA
Hold, the stop's at breakeven
Hold until the gap-day low breaks
Add, the dip is a new entry
questions.story: Your EP has moved fast, riding above its 9 EMA for three weeks. You sold part into the push on the way up. Today it closes under the 9 EMA for the first time.
questions.answer: Sell, it closed under the 9 EMA
questions.why: Sell what's left. A fast mover rides the 9 EMA, and the first close under it is your exit. Three weeks above that line was the run. Losing it says the fast part is likely over. You already sold some into the push, and now you lock in the rest of the gain. A steadier stock gets the 20 EMA instead, which gives it more room. Pick your line before the trade, not after.
questions.lesson_line: Part sold into the push, the rest rides the 9 EMA. The close below it is the exit.

wrong.Hold, the stop's at breakeven: Breakeven is the floor, not the exit plan. The trail decides when the rest goes.
wrong.Hold until the gap-day low breaks: That's way below. You'd hand back most of a three-week run waiting for it.
wrong.Add, the dip is a new entry: A close under the trail is an exit, not an entry. A rare add comes on strength, never on a break.

questions.simple: Sell it. A close under the 9 EMA says the fast run is over, so you keep most of what you made.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi trails the 10- or 20-day average. We use the 9 EMA for a fast mover and the 20 EMA for a steadier one. The lines are close but not the same, so know which one your plan names before the stock moves.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)
held decision D-024 (the trail line)

questions.q: It's been ten trading days. What's the call?
choices: Sell, under 1R after 10 days
Hold, the stop hasn't been hit
Hold, the next report will lift it
Sell half, trail the rest
questions.story: You bought a delayed EP entry. Ten trading days later it sits at 0.4R. It never got near the stop, and it never really went anywhere.
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days gets sold, and this one's at 0.4R. The EPs that work tend to go fast: among the winners in our scan, the median time to 3R was 2 sessions. The money stuck in a dead one could be in the next good setup. The stop protects you from a big loss. The clock protects you from wasting time.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The trade had its chance. Free the money.

wrong.Hold, the stop hasn't been hit: The stop's one exit. The clock is the other, and it just went off.
wrong.Hold, the next report will lift it: Hoping on a report isn't a plan. The clock already says sell.
wrong.Sell half, trail the rest: There's nothing to trail. The time stop sells the whole thing.

questions.simple: Sell. It's still under 1R after 10 trading days, so the money is better used in a stock that's moving.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, time stop)
ours and Bonde's clocks differ

deeper.counter: Bonde was stricter: the stock should move within 5 days of the EP, or you go on to the next opportunity.

questions.q: A+, A, B or B-?
choices: B- at best; over 25%
A+; everything else is perfect
A; the volume saves it
No trade; a gap that big is banned
questions.story: A neglected stock gaps 32% on 20x volume and closes at the high, the first such day in a year.
questions.why: B- at best. A gap over 25% is graded down, not banned. Bonde: if the gaps are more than 20% the stocks pull back most of the time; smaller gaps are better.
questions.lesson_line: The biggest gaps are often one-day moves. Size them small.

wrong.A+; everything else is perfect: The rest is A+ and the gap size is not. The grade is the weakest line.
wrong.A; the volume saves it: Volume grades the day up, the gap size grades it down. The card calls it B- at best.
wrong.No trade; a gap that big is banned: Graded down, not banned. The card's own words are B- at best.

questions.q: Which gap has more to stand on?
choices: The first, faster growth and a raise
The second, steadier growth lasts longer
Same thing, a beat is a beat
Neither, growth doesn't matter
questions.story: Two neglected stocks gap on earnings the same morning. One shows sales up 140%, a beat and a raised outlook. The other shows sales and earnings up 20%, with a beat.
questions.answer: The first, faster growth and a raise
questions.why: The first one. Sales up 140% with a beat and a raised outlook is a business that just changed. That gives the new price something real to stand on, and buyers who missed it have a reason to keep coming. Up 20% with a beat is fine, just not a surprise of the same size. We like growing sales and earnings. Still, the chart comes first, and growth only makes a good chart better.
questions.lesson_line: The bigger the change in the business, the more the gap has to stand on.

wrong.The second, steadier growth lasts longer: Steady is fine, but it's not the kind of surprise that re-prices a stock overnight.
wrong.Same thing, a beat is a beat: A beat on 20% growth isn't in the same league as 140% growth with a raise.
wrong.Neither, growth doesn't matter: It matters. The chart comes first, but real growth gives the gap a reason to hold.

questions.simple: The first. Much faster growth and a raised outlook give the new price more to stand on.

reasons: rests on proposed grading cues (c09)
grading is discretionary (E50), so the stem asks for the card's cues

deeper.counter: Kullamagi: ideally triple-digit year over year earnings and sales growth, but mid to high double digits works really well too. Bonde tracked only companies with earnings up 100% or more.

questions.q: What do you do with the position?
choices: Sell a big part into the strength
Hold, the trail is the only exit
Add, momentum is strongest here
Sell it all at tomorrow's open
questions.story: Your EP is up 6R after five straight up days. Two of them gapped up, and each day's range was wider than the last.
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the strength
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. Five straight up days, gaps, ranges getting wider every day: that's a climax run. Runs like this tend to end fast. When they turn, the trail sits way too far below to save much of the 6R. So you sell into the strength while buyers are still lining up. How much is a judgment call. Keep a piece on with the trail in case it keeps going.
questions.lesson_line: When your EP goes vertical, sell into it. The trail will be too late.

wrong.Hold, the trail is the only exit: Most of the time, yes. A climax is the exception, because the trail sits too far under a vertical move.
wrong.Add, momentum is strongest here: Never into a climax. That's about the worst spot there is to buy more.
wrong.Sell it all at tomorrow's open: Sell into the strength while it's here. And a big part, not all of it, is the call.

questions.simple: Sell a big part now. Runs like this end fast, so bank the gain while buyers are still there.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34), a judgment call

deeper.counter: Bracco's parabolic burst is the picture: straight up days, overnight gap ups and ranges getting wider. ChartSchool notes that exhaustion gaps happen near the end of a good trend.

questions.q: Same gap, same volume. Which one do you want?
choices: The flat one, the other already ran
The one up 70%, strength begets strength
Neither, 12% is too small a gap
Both, the gap days are identical
questions.story: Two 12% earnings gaps on 5x volume, both closing strong. One stock was flat for eight months. The other was already up 70% in the last six months.
questions.answer: The flat one, the other already ran
questions.why: The flat one. Eight months flat means nobody was set up for this news. The gap is the whole market re-pricing it at once, and there's room to run. The stock up 70% had people buying ahead of time. A lot of the good news was already in the price, so the same gap has less fuel. On the gap day they look identical. The months before tell you which one has the edge.
questions.lesson_line: Same gap, same volume, different trade. Look at the months before.

wrong.The one up 70%, strength begets strength: For a leader setup, maybe. For an EP, a 70% run means the news is partly priced in already.
wrong.Neither, 12% is too small a gap: 12% is plenty for an EP. The months before the gap are what separate these two.
wrong.Both, the gap days are identical: The gap days match. The stocks don't. One was forgotten, one was already bid up.

questions.simple: The flat one. The stock up 70% already had buyers in it, so less of the news is new.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi: it's best if the stock has not rallied over the past 3 to 6 months. Bonde: Episodic Pivots at the beginning of a move are more valuable than later ones.

reasons: provisional card reading of the up-50% row (picked 2026-11-10)

questions.q: You've got a $40,000 account and risk 0.5%. Fill 34.89, stop 33.96. How many shares?
questions.why: 215 shares. Start with the dollars: 0.5% of 40,000 is $200 at risk. Then the stop: 34.89 minus 33.96 is 0.93 a share. 200 divided by 0.93 is 215.05, so round down to 215. The stop sits about 2.67% under the fill, a normal EP stop. If it hits, you lose about $200, half a percent of the account. That's the whole point. You decide the loss first, and the shares fall out of the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Decide the loss first. The shares fall out of the stop.
questions.simple: Risk $200, divide by the 0.93 between fill and stop, and round down. That's 215 shares.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
fixed before (the cap broke at 1% risk)

choices: 430 shares
2,150 shares
215 shares
5 shares

wrong.430 shares: That doubles your risk. You used twice the 0.5% you set.
wrong.2,150 shares: A decimal slip. That made your risk dollars ten times too big.
wrong.5 shares: That divided the $200 by the share price. Divide by the distance to the stop, 0.93.

questions.story: Bought on the day-three break of the post-gap high.

questions.q: What would you call this day?
choices: An HVE, record volume, no gap
An EP, the record volume is enough
Nothing, up 9% is too small
An EP, it closed in the upper half
questions.story: A stock closes up 9% on the most shares it has ever traded in a day. It opened flat; there was no gap.
questions.answer: An HVE, record volume, no gap
questions.why: A High Volume Edge. Record volume on an up day is an HVE, gap or no gap. An EP needs the gap. The gap is the news re-pricing the stock overnight, before anyone can trade it. This one opened flat and climbed all day, so the market didn't re-price it at the open. Mark that close as a level, and watch how it acts around it the next day.
questions.lesson_line: Record volume with no gap is an HVE. The gap is what makes it an EP.

wrong.An EP, the record volume is enough: Volume's half of it. An EP is a big opening gap on volume, and this one opened flat.
wrong.Nothing, up 9% is too small: It's not nothing. A record-volume day is an HVE, a level worth marking.
wrong.An EP, it closed in the upper half: A strong close helps, but without a gap it can't be an EP.

questions.simple: An HVE. An EP needs an overnight gap from the news, and this day opened flat.

reasons: card tell between two setups

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A Kicker, small gap, no news
An EP, the gap held all day
An EP, the red day was neglect
Nothing, a gap needs news
questions.story: A stock closes weak and red. The next morning it gaps 2% up on no news and keeps going.
questions.answer: A Kicker, small gap, no news
questions.why: A Kicker. A weak red close, then a small gap up the next morning that keeps going. That's the Kicker, and it doesn't need news. An EP is a big gap on named news, and the day before can be any color. Here there's no news at all and only a 2% gap. So it's not an EP, and you'd trade it with the Kicker's plan instead.
questions.lesson_line: Check the day before and name the news. No news and a small gap: that's a Kicker.

wrong.An EP, the gap held all day: Holding the gap isn't enough. An EP needs named news, and there wasn't any.
wrong.An EP, the red day was neglect: One red day isn't months of neglect. That red close is the Kicker's tell.
wrong.Nothing, a gap needs news: A Kicker doesn't need news. It's its own setup.

questions.simple: A Kicker. A red close and a small gap with no news can't be an EP, which needs real news.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: What's this day telling you?
choices: A News Failure, no long here
An EP, the gap and news count
An EP, buy tomorrow's reclaim
Nothing, wait for the next report
questions.story: A neglected stock gaps 12% on a strong report, sells off all day on heavy volume, and closes under yesterday's close.
questions.answer: A News Failure, no long here
questions.why: It's a News Failure. Great report, 12% gap, and the stock still closed under yesterday's close. The market either doesn't believe the news, or holders were waiting to sell into it. Every buyer from the gap is now under water. An EP holds the gap and closes strong. Same headline, opposite read. No long here.
questions.lesson_line: Read the close against yesterday's close. Red on good news is the failure.

wrong.An EP, the gap and news count: They did at the open. The close erased both. A gap that sells off isn't an EP.
wrong.An EP, buy tomorrow's reclaim: There's no gap left to reclaim. It closed under the prior close.
wrong.Nothing, wait for the next report: It's not nothing. Red on good news is a warning worth noting.

questions.simple: A News Failure. Good news, then a close under the prior close, which is the opposite of an EP.

reasons: card tell between two setups

questions.q: Bonde says an EP has to be a young, small company.
questions.why: False. Bonde says the most explosive EPs come from young companies under $10 billion. Most explosive isn't the only kind. He also notes widely covered names don't do as well, so small and young is where you hunt hardest. But a bigger stock can still be an EP if it was ignored for months and the surprise is real. Don't skip a good one just because of its size.
questions.lesson_line: Young and small run hardest. They aren't the only EPs.
questions.simple: False. Young, small names run hardest, but a bigger stock that was ignored can still be an EP.

deeper.counter: Bonde also says earnings breakouts on companies with significant analyst coverage do not do as well. That is a tilt toward small names, not a ban on large ones.

reasons: cue, not a gate; two sources agree

questions.q: How many of the six do you buy this week?
choices: A few, more as they work
All six, Green is full risk
None, wait for the indexes
Just one, EPs are risky now
questions.story: A correction just ended and the app's market filter turned Green, which allows full risk. Earnings season is on, and six neglected names gapped on reports this week.
questions.answer: A few, more as they work
questions.why: A few, then more as they work. The first Green after a correction can be a head fake. Buy all six, it fails, and six stops hit together. Start with a few of the best. If they work, the market's telling you the turn is real, and you add more names. If they fail, you lost a little and you're still mostly in cash. Let the market earn your exposure.
questions.lesson_line: A few first, more as they work. Let the market earn your exposure.

wrong.All six, Green is full risk: Full risk is the ceiling, not where you start. After a correction you earn your way up.
wrong.None, wait for the indexes: Green is the confirmation. EPs are among the first longs to try as a correction ends.
wrong.Just one, EPs are risky now: One's too timid. Start with a few of the best ones.

questions.simple: A few. The first Green can fail, so start small and add more names only as the first ones work.
