deeper.trap: The trap is reading Green as all in. Green allows full risk per grade, but right after a correction we start with a few names and add more only as the first ones work. Bonde: after months of correction you can find 50 to 100 opportunities in an earnings season, so there's no rush to take them all at once.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F68)

questions.q: You took the stop. How do you read this loss?
choices: A strong gap that just failed
Your stop was set too tight
The gap was too big to buy
The volume was too thin
questions.story: A big name gaps 18.2% on 13.1x volume when it names a new CEO, closing at 98% of its range. Day four, an inside-day break at 94.97, stop 92.93. The next day takes the stop.
questions.answer: A strong gap that just failed
questions.why: A strong gap that just failed. SBUX did everything right on the gap day: 18.2% on 13.1x volume, closing at 98% of its range. You bought the inside-day break at 94.97 with the stop at 92.93. It never followed through and took the stop the next day. That's about a 1R loss, exactly what you planned. The stop isn't there because you'll be wrong. It's there because some strong gaps fail, and you can't tell which ahead of time.
questions.lesson_line: Some strong gaps fail. The stop is how you afford to find out.

wrong.Your stop was set too tight: A few cents under the trigger day's low is our stop. It kept the loss near 1R. That's the plan working.
wrong.The gap was too big to buy: A big gap that holds and closes near the high is what we want. Size wasn't the issue.
wrong.The volume was too thin: 13.1x the average is heavy volume. That wasn't the problem.

questions.simple: A strong gap that failed. The stop did its job and kept the loss to about 1R.

deeper.example: SBUX, 2024-08-13: an 18.2% gap on 13.1x volume on the new-CEO news, closing at 98% of its range. The day-4 break at 94.97 with the stop at 92.93 was stopped the next day, and its best run was 0.0R. The stop made the loss cheap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4 and B21)
dossier scan numbers (28% and 41%)
reworded before

questions.q: You got stopped out, and months later the stock takes off. What's the takeaway?
choices: Right stock, the first buy failed
Buy it back right away
Drop the stock, it failed once
The stop should have been wider
questions.story: A 17.2% earnings gap on 4.4x volume. You buy the day-3 break of the post-gap high at 22.01, stop 21.46. The next session takes the stop. Months later the stock makes a far larger move.
questions.answer: Right stock, the first buy failed
questions.why: Right stock, the first buy just failed. You bought the day-3 break at 22.01 with the stop at 21.46, and the next session took it. Small loss, about 1R. Months later TSLA made a far bigger move. A stop-out isn't a verdict on the stock. It's one entry that didn't work. You buy it again only on a new trigger, as a new trade with its own stop. Buying back right away is hope, not a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out isn't a verdict on the stock. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.The stop should have been wider: Wider only means a bigger loss. The stop kept it near 1R, which is its job.
wrong.Buy it back right away: Only a new trigger gets you back in. Right away is hope talking.
wrong.Drop the stock, it failed once: One stop-out says nothing final. TSLA went on to a much larger move.

questions.simple: The stock was fine, the first buy failed. Wait for a new trigger and treat it as a new trade.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging the stock by one trade. TSLA, 2019-10-24: the day-3 break at 22.01 was stopped the next session, 0.0R, yet the stock went on to a far larger move months later. The trade can fail while the idea is right. You wait for the next trigger instead of chasing or giving up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21)

questions.q: Looking back, what was the soft spot in this one?
choices: The 19% run before the report
How big the earnings gap was
The volume on the gap day
Where it closed in the day's range
questions.story: A 13.0% earnings gap on 7.4x volume, closing at 86%, on a stock up 19% over the prior six months. The day-3 break at 35.16 reaches 0.51R, then the stop at 34.16 goes.
questions.why: The 19% run before the report. Everything else was strong: a 13.0% gap, 7.4x volume, a close at 86%. But up 19% in six months, it was the least neglected of the four failures in our scan. Part of the news was already in the price. That may not be why it failed, and a soft spot isn't proof. The day-3 break hit 0.51R, gave it back, and the stop at 34.16 kept the loss near 1R.
questions.lesson_line: A trade can look right everywhere and still fail. The stop keeps it small.

wrong.The volume on the gap day: 7.4x the average is heavy. Volume wasn't it.
wrong.Where it closed in the day's range: 86% of the range is near the high. The close was strong.
wrong.How big the earnings gap was: 13.0% is a big gap. That wasn't the problem.

questions.simple: The 19% run before the report. Part of the news was already in the price.

deeper.trap: Passing every rule is not a promise of a win. GOOGL, 2015-07-17: a 13.0% gap on 7.4x volume, closing at 86%, yet up 19% into the news and the least neglected of the four failures. It reached 0.51R and gave it back. The stop made it a small loss.

reasons: soft label: the card's up-50% row does not apply to +19%
fixed before

questions.q: By the card's grade line, how do you size that trade?
choices: Small; B- at best, so sized down
Full; neglect plus volume is A+
Sized up; the biggest gaps run most
Not at all; a 28.5% gap is banned
questions.story: A stock down 31% over six months gaps 28.5% on earnings on 15.0x volume, closing at 97%. You buy the day-2 break at 42.01, stop 40.97.
questions.answer: Small; B- at best, so sized down
questions.why: Small. A gap over 25% is graded down to B- at best, and a B- or lower is sized down. Here the gap was 28.5%. The neglect was textbook, with the stock down 31% over six months, but the gap size was the warning. Bonde also says gaps over 20% pull back most of the time. A big gap is graded down, not banned.
questions.lesson_line: The grade sets the size. A B- EP gets a small position.

wrong.Full; neglect plus volume is A+: The gap over 25% caps the grade at B- at best, and B- is sized down.
wrong.Not at all; a 28.5% gap is banned: Graded down, not banned. Small size is the answer, not no trade.
wrong.Sized up; the biggest gaps run most: Bonde: gaps over 20% pull back most of the time. Smaller gaps are better.

questions.simple: Small. A gap over 25% grades no higher than B-, and a B- trade is sized down.

deeper.trap: Good neglect does not lift a big gap. ANF was down 31% over six months and closed at 97% on 15.0x volume. Yet the 28.5% gap was over the 25% line, and it reversed the next session. One example does not prove the rule. It shows why the grade is lower.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (ep.gap_too_big)
the scan runs against the line
answer over 30 characters

questions.q: Would you buy this gap day?
choices: No, it faded, a watch at most
Yes, the gap held, so it counts
Yes, buy the close, gap is support
No, the volume was too light
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. An 18.1% earnings gap on 4.6x volume. The day never trades back to the prior close, but it closes at 32% of its range.
questions.answer: No, it faded, a watch at most
questions.why: No. The gap held, since it never traded back to the prior close. But look at where it closed: 32% of the range, down in the lower third. Buyers ran it up at the open and sellers took the day back. We want both on an EP: the gap stays open and the close is strong. This one goes on the watch list for a delayed reaction at most. MU's would-be buy at the close got stopped.
questions.lesson_line: The gap held and the buyers left. That's a watch, not a buy.

wrong.Yes, the gap held, so it counts: Holding the gap is one test. The close is the other, and this one closed near the low.
wrong.Yes, buy the close, gap is support: We don't buy closes. And a weak close says the buyers already left.
wrong.No, the volume was too light: 4.6x is heavy volume. The close is what failed.

questions.simple: No. The gap held, but it closed near the low, so the sellers won the day.

deeper.trap: MU, 2024-09-26: the gap held, since the low of 107.53 stayed above the prior close of 95.77, so a quick look says EP. The close at 32% of the range says the buyers left. Both must hold: the gap stays open and the close is strong.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: Can you take the day-2 break here?
choices: No, it's under the 200-day
No, a 66% close is too weak
Yes, the gap and volume qualify
Yes, the 200-day will turn up
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. A stock down 17% over six months gaps 12.1% on earnings on 3.6x, closing at 66%. The day-2 break would fill at 161.21. The 200-day sits at 168.35.
questions.why: No. The break fills at 161.21, and the 200-day sits up at 168.35. Below the 200-day we don't buy stocks, and that's a hard line. A stock under it is in a downtrend, so you'd be buying against the long-term trend. The gap and the volume were fine. The location wasn't. AMZN took the stop on that break.
questions.lesson_line: Neglected stocks often sit under the 200-day. No long until price is over it.

wrong.No, a 66% close is too weak: 66% is a decent close. The problem is where the buy sits, under the 200-day.
wrong.Yes, the gap and volume qualify: The gap day passed. The location didn't. No longs under the 200-day.
wrong.Yes, the 200-day will turn up: Maybe someday. The test is price over the 200-day when you buy, not a guess.

questions.simple: No. The buy is under the 200-day, and we don't buy stocks below it.

deeper.trap: Neglected stocks often live under the 200-day, so this rule can say no to a gap that looks perfect. The test is price at the buy, not the picture of the gap day. AMZN, 2022-02-04: a 12.1% gap on 3.6x, closed at 66%, and the break at 161.21 was stopped, 0.0R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
a held decision (D-020)

questions.q: EP or Power Earnings Gap?
choices: A PEG; not neglected
An EP; the gap and volume are A+
An EP; 25.5% is close enough
Neither; a leader cannot gap
questions.story: A software leader near its highs gaps 16.6% on earnings on 11.2x volume, closing at 80%. It was up 25.5% over the prior 126 sessions and 19.3% over the prior 63.
questions.why: A Power Earnings Gap. Up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63; the neglect line is at most 25% and 15%. An established leader at highs gapping on a report is the PEG.
questions.lesson_line: A leader at highs gapping on earnings is a PEG. Measure the six months to know.

wrong.An EP; the gap and volume are A+: The day is A+ for either setup. The stock before it decides, and it was not neglected.
wrong.An EP; 25.5% is close enough: Close enough is over, and the 63-session line fails by more. Measured, not eyeballed.
wrong.Neither; a leader cannot gap: Leaders gap on reports all the time. That is the PEG.

questions.q: You're in at 227.60, stop 224.95. The next session it trades 235.55. Where's the trade, and what can you do?
questions.answer: Up 3.0R, stop can go to breakeven
questions.why: Up 3.0R, and the stop can come up to breakeven. One R is your risk: 227.60 minus 224.95 is 2.65 a share. The gain is 235.55 minus 227.60, so 7.95. 7.95 over 2.65 is 3.0R. Anywhere from 2R to 5R we can move the stop to breakeven, and then a pullback can't turn this into a loss. Don't sell just because it hit 3R, though. It's the day after you bought, and we almost never sell on day 1.
questions.lesson_line: Count the gain in R. From 2R to 5R the stop can move to breakeven.
questions.simple: Divide the 7.95 gain by the 2.65 risk to get 3.0R. In that range the stop can go to breakeven.

deeper.trap: 3R is a measuring mark, not a sell signal. The first sell is a judgment, and we very rarely sell on day 1 of the buy.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, first trim)

choices: Up 3.0R, stop can go to breakeven
Up 8.0R, time to sell it all
Up 4.0R, too soon for breakeven
Up 0.3R, too soon to move the stop

wrong.Up 8.0R, time to sell it all: That's the 7.95 gain in dollars, not divided by your 2.65 risk. And selling it all this early is a mistake.
wrong.Up 4.0R, too soon for breakeven: You measured from the stop, not your fill. It's 3.0R, inside the breakeven window.
wrong.Up 0.3R, too soon to move the stop: You flipped the division. Gain over risk, not risk over gain.

questions.story: Bought on the day-three break after an earnings gap.

questions.q: How do you handle the first sell on this one?
choices: On judgment, day 3 or later
A third right now, at 3R
All of it now, 3R is the target
None, hold it all for the big run
questions.story: A news EP after the election: a 14.2% gap on 3.9x. You bought the day-3 break at 259.70, stop 257.10. The next session it's already up 3R.
questions.why: On judgment, and not today. We almost never sell on day 1 after the buy. Most of the time we wait until day 3 at the earliest. Then we sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R. That's when the stock is handing you strength. COIN ran to 34R, then fell back to the stop in December. Holding everything for the big run would have cost you the whole move.
questions.lesson_line: Sell part into strength, on judgment. The EP you never sold is the one that hurts.

wrong.A third right now, at 3R: A fixed third at 3R isn't how we sell. Day 1 is almost always too early.
wrong.All of it now, 3R is the target: Selling it all in the first day or two is a named mistake. You miss the trend.
wrong.None, hold it all for the big run: COIN gave it all back after 34R. Selling some into strength is what keeps the gain.

questions.simple: On judgment, later. We sell part into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, because a big run can give it all back.

deeper.trap: The 34R figure is a trap. It was the peak, not a plan. No one knows the peak in advance, so we sell part into strength on judgment and trail the rest.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
the owner often waits for 5R on the first trim

questions.q: What kept this trade a win?
choices: The trims and the 10-day trail
Holding the original stop
Widening the stop to give it room
Selling everything at 3R
questions.story: You bought the day-3 break at 227.60, stop 224.95. 3R came the next session. Weeks later the stock tops, rolls over and collapses through your original stop.
questions.why: The trims and the 10-day trail. A third comes off at 3R and a third at 5R. The last third trails the 10-day while the stock moves fast. This stock topped and collapsed through the original stop, so a plan with only that stop gives the move back. It was ENPH, bought 2021-10-29 at 227.60, and its best run reached 20.7R.
questions.lesson_line: Fast movers get the 10-day. By the time the stop is hit, two thirds are gone.

wrong.Holding the original stop: Holding only the original stop means the whole position exits at the stop, so the gain is given back.
wrong.Selling everything at 3R: A third comes off at 3R. Selling everything misses the run to 20.7R and the multi-week trend.
wrong.Widening the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. A looser stop does not bank anything.

questions.simple: The trims and the 10-day trail kept it a win, because they banked gains before the stock fell through the stop.

deeper.example: ENPH: the buy was 227.60 with the stop at 224.95, only 1.2% away, and 3R came the next session. Later the stock topped and collapsed through that stop, yet its best run reached 20.7R. A plan with trims banked part of that run. A plan with one stop gave it back.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51, E52 and B19)
held decision D-024 (the trail line)

questions.q: Do you hold it through the report?
choices: No, only if it's up 5R
No, only if it's up 3R
Yes, the last one was a surprise
Sell half, hold the rest through
questions.story: Your EP from last quarter's report is up 2R. The next report is tomorrow after the close.
questions.why: No. We hold through a report only if the trade's up 5R, and you're up 2R. A report can gap the stock right through your stop, and the stop can't save you overnight. At 2R, one bad gap can take the whole gain and more. At 5R you've got enough cushion to take that hit. Last quarter's surprise doesn't protect you this time. Be out before the report hits.
questions.lesson_line: A report is a gap you can't stop. 5R buys the ticket.

wrong.No, only if it's up 3R: 3R isn't the line. You need 5R of cushion to hold through a report.
wrong.Yes, the last one was a surprise: One good report says nothing about the next. The gap risk is the same.
wrong.Sell half, hold the rest through: Half still rides through the report at 2R. That's under the 5R line.

questions.simple: No. We only hold through a report when we're up 5R, and this is up 2R.

deeper.trap: The rule has two halves. No new buys in the 3 days before a report. Hold through one only if up 5R. Do not mix them up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
one cited fact only

questions.q: Do you buy it?
choices: No, stay in cash and track it
No, a 15% gap is too big
Yes, full size, EPs beat bad markets
Yes, Red still allows an A+
questions.story: The app's market filter reads Red. A neglected stock gaps 15% on a blowout report, on 8x volume, and holds all day.
questions.answer: No, stay in cash and track it
questions.why: No. Put it on your list and track it. Red on the app's market filter means mostly cash. That's a guide, not a hard wall. But in a market that weak, even great setups fail more often, because the market drags everything down with it. That doesn't make this stock bad. Watch its RS line against the market. If it holds up while the market is weak, that's a name you want when the filter turns.
questions.lesson_line: In a Red market a great EP goes on the list, not in the account.

wrong.No, a 15% gap is too big: 15% isn't too big. The market's the reason you hold back.
wrong.Yes, full size, EPs beat bad markets: Some EPs work in bad markets. We still follow the filter, and Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Yes, Red still allows an A+: That's Orange. Red is mostly cash.

questions.simple: No. Red means mostly cash, so you track the stock and wait for the market to get better.

deeper.counter: The sources disagree. Bonde finds opportunities even in bear markets. Bulkowski buys the earnings breakout only when the market and industry trend higher. Our rule follows the Red reading: mostly cash and shorts, a guide and not a hard cap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, the market reading)
sources disagree

questions.q: Day four, it's breaking the inside day's high. What's the play?
choices: Buy, stop under the inside-day low
Pass, day four is too late
Buy, stop under the gap-day low
Wait for the gap-day high to break
questions.story: A stock gaps 12.0% on earnings on 5.7x. Two days hold above the gap-day low. Day three is an inside day, trading inside day two's range. Day four it trades over the inside day's high, 59.91, and the inside day's low is 2.3% below.
questions.answer: Buy, stop under the inside-day low
questions.why: Buy it, with the stop a few cents under the inside day's low. The gap held for two days, so the delayed entry is live. Then day three went quiet, an inside day. That tight little range gives you a tight trigger. Its high is 59.91 and its low is 2.3% below, inside the 1 to 3% we like. WING did exactly this and ran to 11.4R at its best. If the break fails, you lose a little.
questions.lesson_line: An inside day after the gap gives you a tight trigger and a tight stop.

wrong.Pass, day four is too late: Not while the gap holds. The delayed entry is a trigger of its own.
wrong.Buy, stop under the gap-day low: That's wider than it needs to be. The inside day's low is right there.
wrong.Wait for the gap-day high to break: That's another trigger, but the inside day came first, and its stop is tighter.

questions.simple: Buy the break of the inside day's high with the stop under its low. The stop is close, so a failure is cheap.

deeper.counter: Not every trigger tests equally. For SBUX the inside-day trigger reached 3R 28% of the time against 41% for the post-gap high break. The inside-day buy is allowed and its stop is tight, but it is the weaker trigger. WING shows it can work: 3R on day 6.

reasons: the delayed-entry window is a held decision (D-084)
the card says trigger day's low, the example used the inside day's low

questions.q: Write your plan. What's the entry and the stop?
choices: Market 52.00, stop 51.55
Limit 51.40, stop 51.15
Market 52.00, stop 51.60
Limit 51.60, stop 51.55
questions.story: A neglected stock gapped 16% on earnings on 5x volume and closed near its high. Day two it opens at 52.00, over the gap-day high of 51.40. Its low so far is 51.60.
questions.why: Market 52.00, stop 51.55. It opened over the gap-day high of 51.40, so that's your trigger, and you buy at market. The low so far is 51.60, and the stop goes a few cents under it, at 51.55. Not right on it. A stop sitting exactly on the low gets hit the second that low is tested again. Write the entry, the stop and the size down before you buy. Then nothing gets decided in a panic.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop and size on paper before you buy. The first sell comes later.

wrong.Limit 51.40, stop 51.15: We buy with market orders. A limit back at the old high may never fill while it runs.
wrong.Limit 51.60, stop 51.55: Entries are market orders. A limit down at the low may never fill while the stock runs.
wrong.Market 52.00, stop 51.60: Right entry, but the stop sits right on the low. Put it a few cents under.

questions.simple: Buy at market at 52.00 with the stop at 51.55, a few cents under the low.

deeper.example: A plan names the entry and the stop before you buy. The first sell is a judgment made later, once the push shows itself.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, F62, B19)
answer over 30 characters

questions.q: Check the volume bar on the gap day. What's it telling you?
choices: Record volume, buyers piled in
Ordinary volume, a small event
Light volume, few buyers cared
Nothing, only price counts
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. A stock drifted sideways to down for a year, then gapped 20.3% on earnings and closed at 82% of its range.
questions.why: Record volume. That bar towers over the whole year before it, 27.6x the average and the biggest on the chart by far. That's what a real surprise looks like: a lot of money had to own it, all at once. Volume like that raises the grade. It isn't a must, though, and it doesn't promise the next leg. DLB went on to run, but plenty of loud gaps don't.
questions.lesson_line: Huge volume is what a real surprise looks like.

wrong.Ordinary volume, a small event: 27.6x the average isn't ordinary. It's the biggest bar on the chart.
wrong.Light volume, few buyers cared: It's the opposite. 27.6x is about as heavy as it gets.
wrong.Nothing, only price counts: Volume tells you how many people cared. It raises the grade, even if it's not a must.

questions.simple: Record volume. A real surprise brings in a flood of buyers, and that raises the grade.

deeper.trap: Do not read volume as a forecast. DLB is the loudest case here and ran 17.1R, but big volume promises nothing about the next one.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (ep.volume_ideal)
Bonde's 20% caution differs from the card's 25%
grading is discretionary (E50), so the stem asks for the card's cues

questions.q: What do you do on day five?
choices: Hold, the stop and clock decide
Sell, five flat days is a fail
Move the stop to breakeven now
Hold, and add as it builds
questions.story: A news gap of 12.1% on 10.3x. You bought the day-2 break at 94.17, stop 93.17. Five days later it has gone nowhere, still above the stop.
questions.answer: Hold, the stop and clock decide
questions.why: Hold. Nothing's broken. The stop hasn't been hit, and the time stop only sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days. At day five, neither one has fired. Sideways above your stop isn't a loss, and boring isn't a sell signal. SIG did exactly this: it stalled a week above the stop, then hit 3R on day 8. Let the rules make the exit, not your boredom.
questions.lesson_line: Sideways above the stop isn't a loss. Let the rules make the exit, not boredom.

wrong.Sell, five flat days is a fail: Five flat days isn't our clock. Ours sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven now: Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R. This trade hasn't moved yet.
wrong.Hold, and add as it builds: We buy the full size at one price. A rare add comes on strength in a working winner, and this one hasn't worked yet.

questions.simple: Hold. The stop hasn't been hit and the 10-day clock hasn't run out, so you let it work.

deeper.trap: Patience has a limit. SIG reached 3R on day 8, but the same flat picture past day 10 and under 1R means sell. The stop and the clock are the rules, not a hunch that it will go.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, time stop)
ours and Bonde's clocks differ

questions.q: The last bar is the gap day. Read the months before it and the candle itself. Is a delayed break worth buying?
choices: Yes, neglect and a strong close
No, it already ran up a lot
No, the gap day closed weak
Yes, but wait for a gap fill first
questions.answer: Yes, neglect and a strong close
questions.why: Yes. Look left: OII was down 19% over six months going in. That's the neglect you want, nobody set up for good news. Then the gap day closed at 85% of its range, near the high, so buyers held it. The gap was 10.5% on 7.4x volume. While the gap holds, a break over the post-gap high is your delayed trigger. It came on day 4.
questions.lesson_line: Months of nothing, then a gap that holds. That's the picture to remember.

wrong.No, it already ran up a lot: Look left again. It was down 19% over six months.
wrong.No, the gap day closed weak: It closed at 85% of its range. That's near the high.
wrong.Yes, but wait for a gap fill first: A gap fill ends the setup. You step aside then, you don't buy.

questions.simple: Yes. Months of nothing, then a gap that closed near the high, so a delayed break is a buy.

deeper.trap: Look left before you look at the gap. A prior run-up, a weak close or a gap that fills would change the answer.

reasons: rests on the dossier's chart read (d07)
a card line (ep.neglect)

questions.q: The gap day is the last bar. The prior close was up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63. EP or pass?
choices: Pass; up into the news, a PEG
Take it; the gap day is A+
Take it; 25.5% is close enough
Pass; the gap day closed too weak
questions.answer: Pass; up into the news, a PEG
questions.why: Pass as an EP. The stock was up 25.5% over 126 sessions and 19.3% over 63, and our neglect line is at most 25% and 15%. An established leader at highs gapping on a report is a Power Earnings Gap, not an EP. The gap day itself was strong, with 11.2x volume and a close at 80% of its range. This was CRM on 2020-08-26.
questions.lesson_line: A big gap on a leader at highs is a PEG. The six months before say so.

wrong.Take it; the gap day is A+: The gap day itself is strong, with 11.2x volume and a close at 80% of its range. The stock before it was up into the news, which is the PEG lesson's trade.
wrong.Take it; 25.5% is close enough: Close enough is over the line, and the 63-session number misses by more. The line is measured, not eyeballed.
wrong.Pass; the gap day closed too weak: The gap day closed at 80% of its range, in the upper half. The close passes and the neglect is what fails.

questions.simple: Pass as an EP. It was up 25.5% over 126 sessions, past the 25% neglect limit, so it is a PEG.

deeper.trap: CRM missed the neglect line by a small margin: 25.5% against 25% over 126 sessions and 19.3% against 15% over 63. A near-miss still fails. The gap day was strong, which is why it looks tempting. Check the six months before the gap first.

reasons: held decision D-002 (earnings gap on a neglected or an established name)
numbers from our own dossier scan
neglect line is a proposed card line

questions.q: After a delayed entry, you can lower your stop to the gap-day low to give it room.
questions.why: False. The stop only moves up. Never down, never wider. Your size came from the first stop. Drop the stop and you're risking more than the plan allowed, on a trade that's already going wrong. That's how a small loss turns into a big one. The one exception is a gap through your stop, where the first 30 minutes decide the new one.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an appointment, not a debate.
questions.simple: False. Your size came from the first stop, so lowering it means risking more than you planned.

deeper.trap: There is one exception, and it is not about nerve. If a stock gaps down through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the new stop. If the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop only moves up)

questions.q: On our card, a gap day must close in the top quarter of its range to count as an EP.
questions.why: False. The gate is a close in the upper half of the range. A close in the top quarter is a grade cue, not a gate. It helps the grade, but a close in the upper half still counts.
questions.lesson_line: Upper half is the gate. Top quarter is a grade cue.
questions.simple: False, because the gap day only has to close in the upper half of its range, and the top quarter is a grade cue.

reasons: card gate versus grade cue

questions.q: When an EP gaps open above your 3R level, you sell a third at the open.
questions.why: False. A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell. We almost never sell on day 1. We'd rather sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R. A gap up at the open is the stock showing you strength. Selling part into a really big gap is fine if you want to. That's a judgment call, though, not a rule.
questions.lesson_line: Price past 3R isn't a sell signal. The first sell is a judgment.
questions.simple: False. A gap past 3R isn't an automatic sell, and the better sells often come later, into a push.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)

questions.q: Average daily volume is 2,000,000 shares. By 10:00 the stock has traded 1,500,000. What multiple of average is that?
questions.why: 0.75 times. Divide the 1,500,000 shares traded by the 2,000,000 average: 1,500,000 / 2,000,000 = 0.75. Our card wants the full average daily volume traded within the first 30 minutes. Anything under a full day's average means the volume is not there, so the day-one buy is off.
questions.lesson_line: Short of a full day's volume by 10:00 means no day-one buy.
questions.simple: 1,500,000 divided by 2,000,000 is 0.75, so the stock has not traded a full average day by 10:00.

reasons: computed key
card line is proposed

wrong.0.25x: That is the part still to trade: one minus 0.75.
wrong.1.33x: Flipped it: the average divided by the volume so far.
wrong.0.43x: Divided by the two volumes added together.

questions.q: What do you do about the day-one buy?
choices: Skip it; the volume is not there
Take it; holding the gap is enough
Half now and half at the close
Buy the close if it holds the gap
questions.story: A stock gaps up on earnings and holds the gap. At 10:00 it has traded only a fifth of its average daily volume.
questions.answer: Skip it; the volume is not there
questions.why: Skip it. On our card, the full average daily volume must trade within the first 30 minutes. A fifth of it is far short. Without that crowd the day-one buy is off, and a held gap alone does not rescue it. Kullamagi: volume is the number one thing.
questions.lesson_line: No crowd in the first 30 minutes, no day-one buy.

wrong.Take it; holding the gap is enough: Volume is the number one thing. A held gap without the crowd can still fill.
wrong.Half now and half at the close: Splitting the buy does not fix missing volume. We buy the full size once, at one price.
wrong.Buy the close if it holds the gap: Our day-one buy is an opening-range buy with the volume on pace, not a close buy.

questions.simple: Skip the day-one buy, because only a fifth of a normal day's volume traded by 10:00 and the crowd is not there.

reasons: reworded before

questions.q: A stock you like reports next week. How many days before the report do new buys stop?
questions.sentence: We make no new buys in the ___ days before an earnings report.
questions.why: 3. No new buys in the 3 days before a report. A report can gap the stock straight through your stop, and the stop can't catch an overnight gap. A brand new trade has no cushion at all, so one bad number and you lose far more than you planned. Once a trade's up 5R, you can hold it through.
questions.simple: 3 days. A report can gap the stock right through your stop, so we don't start new trades just before one.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 days before a report.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Selling your whole EP in the first day or two is a mistake.
questions.why: True. It's one of the mistakes we name. EPs can start moves that run for weeks or months, and that trend is where the real money is. Sell everything on day one or two and you have none of it. We almost never sell on day 1. Sell part later, into a push, and trail the rest.
questions.lesson_line: Don't sell it all in the first day or two. Sell part later and trail the rest.
questions.simple: True. EPs can run for weeks, so selling it all right away throws away the trend.

reasons: named mistake on the card; stable

questions.q: On our card, a gap day that closes 70% of the way up its range earns the top-quarter grade cue.
questions.why: False. A close 70% of the way up sits above the middle, so the day passes the upper-half gate. The top quarter is the last quarter of the range, and 70% falls short of it. On our card the top quarter is a grade cue, not a gate, so this day can still count as an EP.
questions.lesson_line: Upper half is the gate. The top quarter only lifts the grade.
questions.simple: False, because 70% is short of the top quarter, though it still clears the upper half that the gate needs.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (ep.close_top_quarter)
the dossier's scan found no edge in the top quarter over the 50% to 75% band

questions.q: On our card, a delayed trigger that comes after only two green days in a row breaks the three-green guide.
questions.why: False. Our card says not after three green days in a row. Two in a row is short of three, so the guide does not apply here. Even at three, it is a guide, not a gate.
questions.lesson_line: The three-green guide starts at three. Two green days do not trip it.
questions.simple: False, because the card's guide only warns after three green days in a row, and two is short of that.

reasons: rests on a proposed card line (ep.not_three_green) from the 2026-04-19 starter list
the owner has not ruled whether a green day is an up close or a close above the open
the threshold is read from the card's measure, fewer than 3 in a row

questions.q: You buy the opening-range break on day one. Where does the stop go?
choices: A few cents under the day's low so far
Exactly on the day's low so far
A few cents under the prior close
Under the base low from months ago
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low so far
questions.why: A few cents under the low of the day at the time of entry. Stop first: the size comes from the stop. Kullamagi puts the stop at the lows of the day. It goes a few cents past the low, not exactly on it. On a delayed entry it goes under the trigger day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the low of the day.

wrong.Exactly on the day's low so far: Our rule puts the stop a few cents past the low, not exactly on it.
wrong.A few cents under the prior close: After a gap the prior close is far under the day's low, so that stop is wide and the size shrinks. The stop belongs under the day's low.
wrong.Under the base low from months ago: A base low from months ago is far away. The day-one stop sits under the low of the day.

questions.simple: On day one the stop goes a few cents under the day's low at the moment you buy, not exactly on it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62, stop under the day's low)

questions.story: An earnings gap takes a stock from 44.00 to an open of 49.50 on huge volume. The low of the day so far is 49.10. At 9:52 it trades over the 5-minute high and you buy at 50.45.
questions.q: Where's your stop?
choices: A few cents under 49.10
Under 44.00, the prior close
At 49.50, the open
None yet, set it after the close
questions.why: A few cents under 49.10, the low of the day when you bought. If price trades back under the low, the buy failed, and that's where you want out. From a 50.45 fill that's a tight stop, inside the 1 to 3% we like. Put it in as a real stop order with your broker right away. If the low of the day were more than 5% away, you'd wait for a tighter trigger instead.
questions.simple: A few cents under 49.10, the low of the day. If price breaks it, the buy failed.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first. On day one it goes a few cents under the low of the day.

wrong.Under 44.00, the prior close: That's a gap fill. It ends the setup, and it's way past the 5% we'll accept.
wrong.At 49.50, the open: That's above the low, so you moved the stop to fit. Normal noise takes you out.
wrong.None yet, set it after the close: No stop, no trade. It goes in with your broker the moment you're filled.

deeper.counter: Kullamagi: the stop is always at the lows of the day. We put ours a few cents under the low, not exactly on it.

questions.q: EPs fail a lot, so the job is keeping each loss small and letting the winners pay.
questions.why: True. Lots of EPs fail. In our scan all four failures were stopped within two sessions, each for about 1R. The winners paid for all of it: MOD ran to 89.9R at its best. You don't need to be right most of the time. You need small losses and the patience to let the good ones run. A stop a few cents under the low is what keeps the losses small.
questions.simple: True. Many EPs fail, but tight stops keep each loss near 1R while the winners run far.
questions.lesson_line: Keep the losses small and let the winners pay for them.

reasons: two Tier 2 originators agree on a principle

deeper.counter: Kullamagi: none of them work all the time, the failure rate is high, but they all provide excellent risk rewards. Bonde cuts a slow one too: if it doesn't move within 5 days, he goes on to the next. Our clock is 10 trading days under 1R.

questions.q: There was no report that day. Can this still be an EP?
questions.story: The gap day is the last bar. The day after a US election, a stock down 8% over six months gaps 14.2% on 3.9x volume. It closes at 91% of its range. No report was due.
choices: Yes, big news is named news
No, only earnings gaps count
No, news gaps always fill
Yes, any gap on volume counts
questions.answer: Yes, big news is named news

wrong.No, only earnings gaps count: Earnings come first, not only. Big news can re-price a stock too.
wrong.No, news gaps always fill: This one didn't. It closed near the high with the gap wide open.
wrong.Yes, any gap on volume counts: It needs real news behind it. This one had it. A gap on nothing wouldn't count.

questions.why: Yes. An EP needs a named surprise. Earnings come first, but really big news counts too, and here it was the election result. The stock was down 8% over six months, so it was neglected going in. It gapped 14.2% on 3.9x and closed at 91% of its range, gap wide open. COIN's day-3 break hit 3R the next session. We focus on earnings and really big news. Smaller news, much less.
questions.simple: Yes. Big news is a named surprise, and this ignored stock held its gap near the high.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings first, but big news can be the episode too.

reasons: D-032: earnings and really notable news, lesser catalysts only mentioned

deeper.counter: Kullamagi: when unexpected good news hits a stock, especially a neglected one, it can trigger multi-month and multi-year moves.
